opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of pre-training as where most of the raw capability comes from. When you train a model to predict the next token over an enormous slice of human-written text, it has to build a compressed model of the world: facts, the structure of language, how arguments are built, how code runs, how people think through problems. Compression and intelligence are closely linked. To predict text well, you end up modeling the processes that generated it, and a lot of those processes are reasoning.

What pre-training doesn't give you is a model that reliably uses those capabilities in a directed way. A pre-trained model is a kind of simulator. It can continue text in the voice of a careful mathematician or a confused forum poster, and it doesn't have a strong preference between them. The capability is latent but not consistently elicited.

Post-training is how we shape and select from that space. Supervised fine-tuning and preference learning give the model a consistent persona and teach it to follow instructions. More recently, reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes has made a big difference for reasoning. When you let the model think at length and reward it for getting the right answer, it learns to use its thinking time productively. It backtracks, checks its work, and tries alternative approaches. Those behaviors were present in fragments in the pre-training data, but RL amplifies and stabilizes them.

So my rough framing is that pre-training determines the ceiling and the richness of the model's knowledge and intuitions, while post-training determines how much of that the model can reliably reach, and in what style. The interesting shift over the last couple of years is that post-training, especially RL for reasoning, has become a much bigger lever than people expected. It's not just polish anymore. It meaningfully changes what the model can do at test time, particularly when it can spend more compute thinking.

The two also interact. A stronger base model makes RL far more effective, because there's more latent skill to draw out and the model's early attempts are good enough to produce a useful learning signal. I don't see them as competing approaches. They're complementary stages, and the art is getting them to work well together.

r001.rationale: It describes pre-training as modeling human text and as able to simulate careful or confused writers, but does not clearly characterize the learned distribution as encompassing both correct and incorrect reasoning behavior.

r002.rationale: It says that predicting text well requires modeling the processes that generated it, including reasoning, linking better prediction to better modeling of the underlying distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes post-training as shaping and selecting from the pre-trained model’s behavioral space to produce a consistent persona and instruction-following behavior.

r004.rationale: It says reinforcement learning amplifies and stabilizes reasoning behaviors already present in fragments, but does not say that RL builds complex skills by composing primitive skills.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I've come to think about it is that pre-training is where almost all of the knowledge and the raw capability lives, and post-training is where you shape how that capability gets expressed. People sometimes talk about post-training as if it's teaching the model to reason, and I don't think that's quite right. Pre-training is the model reading a very large fraction of what humans have written, and in the process of predicting the next token it's forced to build up a lot of internal structure: facts, associations, procedures, the shape of a mathematical argument, the way a piece of code tends to be laid out. Reasoning, in the sense of being able to chain steps together, is already latent in there because the training data is full of people chaining steps together.

What pre-training doesn't give you is a model that reliably does that on demand. The base model is a kind of superposition of every author on the internet. If you ask it a hard question it might answer like an expert, or it might answer like someone on a forum who's confidently wrong, or it might just continue the question with three more questions. So post-training is really about selecting and amplifying the behaviors you want out of that distribution. Supervised fine-tuning narrows it toward a particular style of response, and then reinforcement learning, especially on verifiable tasks, is where you really start to see the model learn to spend its compute well: to try something, notice it's gone wrong, back up, check its work. That's the thing that feels most like reasoning to people, and a lot of it does come from RL. But I'd stress that RL is mostly reweighting what's already there. If the capability isn't in the pre-trained model, you can't RL your way to it with any reasonable amount of signal. What you can do is make the model much more consistent and much more willing to use what it has.

The other thing I'd say is that the boundary is blurrier than it used to be. Once you have a strong post-trained model, you can use it to generate or filter data that goes back into pre-training, so the next base model starts from a better place. And reasoning traces that come out of RL end up in the pre-training mix. So I think of it less as two separate stages and more as a loop, where pre-training sets the ceiling on what's possible and post-training determines how close to that ceiling you actually get in practice, and each one keeps raising the bar for the other.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training builds reasoning from human-written examples and describes the base model as capable of answering like an expert or a confidently wrong forum user, covering both correct and incorrect behavior.

r002.rationale: It says next-token prediction builds internal structure, but does not connect better prediction to better understanding of the modeled distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes post-training as selecting and amplifying desired behaviors, with supervised fine-tuning narrowing the model toward a response style.

r004.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning improving behaviors such as checking work and backing up, but does not say it builds complex skills by composing primitive skills.

astra-6.text:
I think of pre-training as where the model acquires most of its broad understanding of the world. You’re training it to predict what comes next across a huge range of text, and doing that well requires more than memorizing facts. It requires learning something about the processes that produced that text, including how people reason through problems.

But that objective doesn’t specify the behavior you want from an assistant. A model can be very good at predicting text without reliably answering your question or knowing when to say, “I’m not sure.” Post-training helps shape those capabilities into useful behavior: following instructions, responding appropriately, and producing answers that people actually find helpful.

For reasoning, though, I wouldn’t draw the boundary too sharply and say pre-training supplies all the intelligence and post-training just supplies the personality. Post-training can also improve capabilities. If you reward a model for solving problems correctly, it can learn to use its computation more effectively—to work through intermediate steps, check an approach, and recover from mistakes.

So there’s a distinction between what the model has learned and how it uses that knowledge, but the two stages affect both. And getting a model to produce something that looks like reasoning isn’t necessarily the same as getting it to reason reliably. You want the training signal to favor actually reaching the right answer, rather than just sounding convincing.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training learns how people reason from text, but does not characterize the learned distribution as including both correct and incorrect reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says doing next-token prediction well requires learning about the processes that produced the text, including reasoning, linking better prediction to understanding the modeled distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes post-training as shaping behavior toward usefulness and instruction following, but does not characterize this as narrowing the behavioral distribution to selected modes.

r004.rationale: It says reward can improve problem-solving through intermediate steps, checking, and recovery, but does not say complex skills are built by composing primitive skills.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful starting point is that pre-training gives the model this very broad repertoire of capabilities. In learning to predict text, it learns facts about the world, but also patterns of reasoning: how people solve problems, make arguments, write code, and correct mistakes. So you’re getting much more than a store of knowledge. You’re learning a system that can carry out lots of different computations, depending on the context.

Post-training then shapes how those capabilities get used. Which kinds of questions should the model answer directly? When should it ask for clarification? How much effort should it spend checking its work? You want to take this enormous range of possible behaviors and make the model reliably behave like a useful assistant.

But I wouldn’t draw the distinction too sharply as ‘pre-training teaches capabilities, post-training teaches behavior.’ Post-training, particularly reinforcement learning on problems where you can verify the answer, can also improve reasoning. It can encourage the model to discover more effective ways of solving a problem, rather than simply presenting an existing capability in a nicer format.

And the two stages interact. What the model learns during pre-training affects what it can explore successfully during post-training. Then the post-training objective determines which of those approaches get reinforced. So I think of them as complementary parts of building the same system, rather than separate boxes for intelligence and personality.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training learns patterns of reasoning, but does not say those patterns include both correct and incorrect reasoning behavior.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect better next-token prediction with better understanding of the modeled distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes post-training as shaping which behaviors are used and making the model reliably act as a useful assistant, narrowing its broad range of possible behaviors.

r004.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can improve reasoning, but does not describe building complex skills by composing primitive skills.
